title: How Long, O LORD? From Forsakenness to Song
summary: Four times David asks “How long?”: how long will God forget him, hide his face, leave him wrestling with sorrow, and let his enemy win? He asks God to answer and give light to his eyes before he sinks into death. Then, without any change in circumstances reported, he declares his trust in God's loving devotion and promises to sing, because the LORD has been good to him.
story: Psalm 13 is the shortest of the individual laments in the first book of the Psalter, and in six verses it traces the whole road from despair to praise. The “How long?” first heard in Psalm 6:3 becomes the frame of the entire first half here. Coming after Psalm 12's lament over a corrupt generation, it returns to one person's inner struggle, and the enemy is present but less central than the question of God's absence. The psalm teaches the reader that faith can live through seasons of felt abandonment and that the language of complaint and the language of trust can sit in the same prayer.
historical:
The heading attributes the psalm to David, for the choirmaster, and gives no occasion. Readers have associated it with the long years when Saul pursued David (1 Samuel 19 to 30), when David said to himself that one day he would perish by Saul's hand (1 Samuel 27:1). That fits the psalm's mood well, but the text itself doesn't name a setting. As with the other psalms of Book 1, scholars differ on whether the heading records original authorship or a later association with David.

The psalm's value for worship lies partly in its lack of detail. Because the enemy is unnamed and the trouble undefined, it has been prayed by people in sickness, persecution, depression, and grief across three thousand years.
cultural:
To have God hide his face (“How long will You hide Your face from me?”) was one of the most painful images in Israel's faith. The priestly blessing asked that the LORD make his face shine on his people and lift up his face toward them (Numbers 6:25-26); his face meant his favor and presence. To lose it was to feel abandoned and exposed. The word “forget” carries a similar weight: in Hebrew, to remember someone is not only to recall them but to act on their behalf, as God remembered Noah and sent the wind (Genesis 8:1). To be forgotten by God is to be left without help.

Verse 3 asks God to “give light to my eyes”. In the ancient world, bright eyes were a sign of life and vigor, and dimmed eyes a sign of weakness, sickness, or approaching death (compare 1 Samuel 14:27-29, where Jonathan's eyes brighten after he eats honey). The phrase “sleep in death” uses the common biblical image of death as sleep. The fear that enemies would gloat at one's fall reflects a culture of honor and shame, where public humiliation was a serious harm in itself.
literary: Psalm 13 is a textbook example of the lament form that scholars since Hermann Gunkel have described: complaint (verses 1 and 2), petition (verses 3 and 4), and expression of trust and vow of praise (verses 5 and 6). Each section is shorter than the one before, and the tone lightens as the psalm goes on. The fourfold “How long” in verses 1 and 2 names the problem in three directions: God (forgetting and hiding), the self (wrestling and sorrow), and the enemy (dominating). The petition answers in the same order: consider me, give light to my eyes, don't let my enemy say he has won. The turn comes with the word “But” in verse 5, and the psalm ends with a verb in the past tense: the LORD has been good to me.

outline.t: Petition: answer me before I sleep in death
Trust and praise: I will sing to the LORD

doctrines.note: The psalm gives words for prolonged suffering and for the sense that God has forgotten. It shows that the experience of God's absence is part of the life of faith, not proof of its failure.
The movement from complaint to petition to trust shows prayer as a way through pain rather than around it. David brings his honest feelings to God and there finds a reason to hope.
Verse 5 locates faith not in feelings or circumstances but in God's loving devotion. Trust is chosen in the dark, on the basis of who God has shown himself to be.

words.note: Shakach, to forget. The psalmist asks whether God will forget him forever. The word is strong: it suggests neglect, abandonment, and the withdrawal of care. In Psalms 9 and 10 the same verb was used of the wicked forgetting God and of the claim that God has forgotten. Here a faithful man asks the same question in anguish.

Chesed, loving devotion, God's loyal, covenant-keeping love. Verse 5 turns on this word: “But I have trusted in Your loving devotion”. When feelings say God has forgotten, the psalmist leans on the character God has revealed in his covenant promises.

Yeshuah, salvation or deliverance. It usually means concrete rescue from danger rather than an abstract spiritual state. The psalmist says his heart will rejoice in God's salvation before it has arrived, trusting it as certain. The name Jesus (Yeshua in Hebrew) comes from the same root, meaning the LORD saves.

christ: Jesus entered the experience this psalm describes. In Gethsemane he said that his soul was sorrowful even to the point of death (Mark 14:34), and on the cross he cried out the opening words of Psalm 22, asking why God had forsaken him. Psalm 13 is not a prophecy of those moments, but it gives words to the same abandonment, and the New Testament presents Jesus as the one who went through it fully and was vindicated in resurrection. For Christians, that gives a new ground for verse 5: the loving devotion of God has been shown in Christ, and his rising is the pledge that the darkness of “How long?” does not have the last word.

hard.q: How does the psalmist move from despair to trust so quickly? Is the ending forced?
hard.a: Readers have often been struck by how fast the mood changes between verse 4 and verse 5. Some think the psalm reflects a worship setting in which a priest or prophet spoke a word of assurance after the lament. Others see the change as happening inside the one praying, as naming the pain honestly before God opens space to remember his faithfulness. Still others note that the psalm compresses what in real life may take a long time, giving the full shape of a prayer that may be prayed many times before the ending feels true. The ending is not a denial of the complaint; the complaint stays in the psalm. Trust is spoken alongside it, not in place of it.

questions: Which of the four “How long” questions in verses 1 and 2 feels closest to your own experience right now or in the past?
Verse 5 begins with “But”. What truths about God have helped you turn from complaint to trust, even before circumstances changed?
How might a church or small group make room for prayers like this, which begin in real distress, instead of rushing to the happy ending?
